# Agent Tools for People Who Do Not Open a Terminal

Developer tooling gets most of the attention in the agent conversation, but this batch of Show HN launches is pointed somewhere else entirely: at designers, at sole proprietors doing their own books, at investors who want the case against their own idea, at analysts who are tired of confident paragraphs. What the better ones share is that they show their work rather than producing an answer and asking to be trusted.

## One assistant instead of twelve tabs

[[link:/tools/1921|Kucedr]] is a desktop AI assistant that adapts to the task rather than to a single workflow. You can write, research, code, or create images, audio and video, bringing your own files and choosing your own models. It ships with chat, agent and voice modes, extendable apps, MCP servers, skills and models, and more than twenty tools covering file, media and memory work. It runs on macOS, Linux and Windows under MIT, which is unusual for a product this broad.

[[link:/tools/1927|Ida]] is narrower and more interesting for it: a voice layer for your Mac. It performs voice actions that work across your existing apps rather than living in one window, with documented use cases covering working through email, creating events and hands-free workflows. Voice products usually fail by becoming another place you have to go; this one is pitched as a layer over where you already are.

## Where the design actually happens

[[link:/tools/1926|Grafista]] is a content-first AI design platform, which is a meaningful departure from prompt-first image generation. You add your text, images and branding, pick a size and instructions or choose a Blueprint, and get complete editable designs with layout, spacing and decorations handled. Output is editable rather than a flat image, and it works in any language, which matters more than most tools admit.

[[link:/tools/1936|Chitra Studio]] covers generation across images, video, voices, music and sound effects from more than sixty models on the Mac, and the detail worth copying is that the credit cost sits on the Generate button before you press it and updates as you change model, length or resolution. Knowing the price before the click is the kind of small honesty that changes how people use a tool. It is free for fourteen days with fifty credits and no card.

## Reading less, and reading what matters

[[link:/tools/1942|Stream Reducer]] turns long videos and podcasts into source-linked reading: key ideas first, deeper notes if you want them, and a link back to the exact moment in the original. Covering YouTube, Bilibili, Apple Podcasts and Xiaoyuzhou, with public summaries readable without an account, it treats the source as part of the output rather than something to discard.

## Money, where being wrong is expensive

[[link:/tools/1931|Koody]] handles cash flow and tax prep for sole proprietors and small businesses, automatically categorising transactions, producing profit and loss reports and preparing Schedule C and accountant-ready records. It works with banks and credit unions that do not connect to finance apps, which quietly expands who the product is for.

[[link:/tools/1933|HedgePick]] is built around a specific and useful idea: hear the case against a stock before you buy it. You type a ticker and optionally why you want it, twelve agents research the company, a bull and a bear argue it out, a risk desk sizes the position and a portfolio manager makes the final call. You get a verdict, the full debate, and the weakest point in your own reasoning, which is the part most tools skip. New debates publish every weekday and three analyses are free without a card.

[[link:/tools/1935|PrimerKit]] takes the same scepticism toward market answers from a general assistant. It is a persistent local workspace where your agent can brief you on what moved, show the exact data lines behind each answer, compare its answer with what the web says, backtest a rule you wrote, run it on your own schedule and place a paper order when you say yes. Showing the lines behind the answer is the whole product.

[[link:/tools/1934|TaskPocket]] closes the batch on the opposite note: a deliberately tiny to-do app for the browser and iPhone that ships with an MCP server instead of built-in AI, so your own agent can manage your list. Seven words in the interface, no method to learn, dates and repeats lifted out of whatever sentence you type.

## What the weaker entries get wrong

It is worth naming the failure mode, because it recurs. The tools here that feel thin are the ones that wrap a model in a friendly interface without changing the job. A chatbot that answers instead of acts, a designer that needs a paragraph of prompt craft, a research answer with no sources: all of those add a step without removing one.

The stronger entries change the shape of the work. Grafista starts from the content you already have rather than from a prompt. Chitra shows the price before you commit. HedgePick hands you the argument against your own position. PrimerKit shows the data lines behind the answer. Each of those removes a step a person was doing by hand, which is the only durable test for whether an AI product is worth the subscription.

The pattern across all nine is restraint. Each one picked a job a person actually has and stayed inside it.
